topic: The DNA of Vector Spaces: Span, Linear Dependence, and Bases

outline.topic: The DNA of Vector Spaces: Span, Linear Dependence, and Bases

sections.title: Prerequisite: Vectors as Movements
sections.content: Briefly recap vectors not just as coordinates, but as 'instructions for movement.' Introduce scalar multiplication (stretching/shrinking) and vector addition (following one instruction after another). Visual: A point starting at the origin, moving along an arrow $\vec{v}$.
sections.example: A delivery drone is told to move 2 units East ($\vec{i}$) and 3 units North ($\vec{j}$). The final position is the vector $2\vec{i} + 3\vec{j}$.

sections.title: Linear Combinations: Mixing the Ingredients
sections.content: Define a linear combination as the result of scaling and adding a set of vectors. Explain the formula $a\vec{v} + b\vec{w}$. Visual: Two vectors $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{w}$ on a grid. Show various points reachable by changing the 'knobs' of scalars $a$ and $b$.
sections.example: An artist mixes blue paint (vector $\vec{B}$) and yellow paint (vector $\vec{Y}$) in different proportions to create various shades of green. Each shade is a linear combination of $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{Y}$.

sections.title: Span: The Reachable Universe
sections.content: The 'Span' is the set of all possible linear combinations of a group of vectors. Visually demonstrate that two non-parallel vectors in 3D space span a flat 2D plane. If they are parallel, they only span a 1D line.
sections.example: A 'Spider-Bot' can only move along two non-parallel silk threads. The entire flat web surface that the bot can traverse is the 'Span' of those two thread vectors.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Helper
sections.content: Introduce linear dependence as 'redundancy.' If one vector can be created by a linear combination of others, it adds nothing to the span. Linear independence means every vector provides a unique direction. Visual: Three arrows in 2D. Show that the 3rd arrow can be built using the first two, making it 'linearly dependent.'
sections.example: A navigation system has three directions: North, East, and North-East. The 'North-East' instruction is redundant (linearly dependent) because you can achieve it by combining North and East.

sections.title: The Basis: The Efficient Blueprint
sections.content: A Basis is the 'Goldilocks' set of vectors: It must span the entire space AND be linearly independent (no redundancy). It is the minimum number of vectors needed to reach every point in the space. Visual: A 3D coordinate system where the x, y, and z axes are highlighted as the standard basis.
sections.example: In a 3D building, you need exactly three directions (Length, Width, Height) to pinpoint any room. Two is not enough (won't span the space); four is too many (one will be dependent). These three 'perfect' instructions form the Basis.

sections.title: Summary & Synthesis
sections.content: Tie all concepts together. Vectors are tools; Linear combinations are how we use them; Span is where they can go; Independence is efficiency; and Basis is the ultimate toolkit. Animation: A grid expanding from two vectors to fill a whole plane.
sections.example: Think of a Basis as the 'Primary Colors' of a vector space. They are independent (you can't make Red from Blue) and they Span the space (you can make any color from them).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Vectors as Movements
lecture_lines: Vectors are instructions for moving through space.
We scale vectors to stretch or shrink their movement.
Adding vectors means following one movement after another.
animations: Draw a vector arrow v from (0,0) to (2,1) in #00FF00; label it 'v' at the tip.
Animate vector v stretching to twice its length, changing color to #FFFF00, labeled '2v'.
Move a new vector w (#0000FF) from origin to the tip of 2v, showing the sum 2v + w.

storyboard.title: Linear Combinations: Mixing the Ingredients
lecture_lines: Combine scaling and addition to reach new locations.
The formula a v + b w represents a linear combination.
Think of vectors as ingredients for a specific recipe.
Adjusting the scalars a and b moves the point.
Every reachable point is a mix of these vectors.
animations: Show vectors v (#00FF00) and w (#0000FF) anchored at the origin.
Scale v by 0.5 and w by 1.5 simultaneously; show dashed lines for the scaled versions.
Show the parallelogram rule to find the resulting vector #FF00FF, labeled '0.5v + 1.5w'.

storyboard.title: Span: The Reachable Universe
lecture_lines: The span is the collection of all reachable points.
Two non-parallel vectors span an entire 2D plane.
If vectors are parallel, their span collapses to a line.
Adding more directions can expand the reachable universe.
Span defines the dimensionality of the subspace.
animations: Draw two vectors v1 (#00FF00) and v2 (#0000FF) with different directions.
Create a 2D grid (#444444) aligned with v1 and v2 that covers the screen.
Animate several points appearing on the grid as different linear combinations of v1 and v2.
Shade the entire background area covered by the grid in #222222, labeling it 'Span'.
Rotate v2 until it overlaps v1; the #222222 area shrinks to a single line (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Helper
lecture_lines: A set is linearly dependent if it contains redundancy.
Redundant vectors can be built from the others.
Linearly independent vectors each provide a unique direction.
Three vectors in 2D space are always linearly dependent.
Independence ensures every vector adds value to the span.
animations: Start with vectors v1 (#00FF00) and v2 (#0000FF) spanning a plane (shaded #222222).
Introduce a third vector v3 (#FFFF00) pointing to a position already in the #222222 span.
Show ghost copies of v1 and v2 scaled and added to reach the tip of v3.
Highlight v3 in #FF0000 and display the text 'Linearly Dependent' next to it.
Remove v3 and show the shaded span (#222222) remains unchanged, proving redundancy.

storyboard.title: The Basis: The Efficient Blueprint
lecture_lines: A basis is a minimal set that spans space.
It must be linearly independent and span the space.
Bases serve as efficient coordinate systems for any vector.
animations: Show two perpendicular vectors i (#FF0000) and j (#00FF00) in 2D space.
Fill the entire screen with a coordinate grid (#444444) based on i and j.
Flash i and j in #FFFFFF to signify they are linearly independent.
Label the pair {i, j} as 'Basis for 2D Space' in #FFFFFF.
Add a third vector k (#0000FF); show it can be formed by i and j, so it's not part of the basis.

storyboard.title: Summary & Synthesis
lecture_lines: Linear combinations create span through independent basis vectors.
A basis is the ultimate toolkit for vector spaces.
Mastering these concepts unlocks the power of linear algebra.
animations: Show a summary screen with the words 'Span', 'Independence', and 'Basis' in #FFFFFF.
Animate a small set of vectors (#00FF00, #0000FF) generating a full grid.
Display the final title 'The DNA of Vector Spaces' in #FFFF00 with a pulse effect.
